newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb president vows to stay in office.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb president vows to stay in office.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic vowed on Monday to stay in office and accused Serb hardliners of kicking her out of the ruling party because she had exposed high-level corruption.
Plavsic was expelled from the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) at the weekend by allies of ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic who also called on her to step down as president.
"I was not suitable for the party because I was merely insisting on resolving the crime problem in the Serb republic," Plavsic said in a televised speech.
"Such widespread crime is the reason why the state cannot pay its workers and pensioners," she said.
Plavsic has been locked in a power struggle with Karadzic's allies ever since she publicly accused them of plundering the territory through vast smuggling rackets.
The SDS has demanded she hand over authority to the vice-president, but Plavsic said she would only step down if she was voted out in a referendum, as required by the constitution.
"I will lead the state in accordance with the Bible and constitution until the people cancel my mandate. My term expires in 1998 and only the people can deprive me of my mandate," she said.

Plavsic had initially refrained from criticising Karadzic directly but the crisis has now become more and more of an open conflict with the ex-president, who wields power covertly from his headquarters in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
The government, which answers to Karadzic, attacked Plavsic on the evening news programme before her speech.
A government statement said Plavsic had helped Western countries demonise Karadzic, who has been charged by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.

"Such a portrayal of the Serb leader helps the international community to arrest and even kill Serb patriots. Her attitude prompted the world media not to talk about Karadzic as a leader of the Serb nation but as a criminal," the statement said.
Earlier this month NATO pounced on two suspected war criminals who were allies of Karadzic. Bosnian Serb media accused Plavsic of causing political turmoil which allowed NATO to strike.

In her campaign against corruption, Plavsic has attracted big crowds at rallies in towns across the country's Serb entity, which together with the Moslem-Croat federation comprises peacetime Bosnia-Herzegovina.
She has dissolved parliament and called new elections for September 1. Karadzic loyalists have refused to recognise her decision and say they will hold a parliamentary session next month.
Karadzic nominated Plavsic, his former protege, as his successor last year when international pressure forced him to quit office because of his fugitive status.
Diplomats say two rival authorities could emerge -- one loyal to Plavsic in the northwestern town of Banja Luka and the other run by Karadzic in Pale, to the southeast.
